title: Exact Power of Four
statement:
Given a 32-bit signed integer n, return true if n = 4k for some integer k ≥ 0, and false otherwise.

Note that 1 = 40 counts. Zero and negative numbers never do.

Try to answer without a loop or recursion.

examples.why: 32 is a power of two (2⁵), but the exponent is odd, so it is not a power of four.

hints: Every power of four is also a power of two. How do you test for a power of two with one bit operation?
A power of two has exactly one bit set: n > 0 && (n & (n − 1)) === 0. For a power of four, where can that single bit be?
4k = 22k, so the bit sits at an even position (0, 2, 4, …). The mask 0x55555555 has exactly those bits set.

explain.intuition:
In binary, 4k is a 1 followed by 2k zeros: 1, 100, 10000, … So a power of four is a power of two whose single set bit is at an even position.

The power-of-two test is the classic n & (n − 1): subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and every zero below it, so the AND is zero exactly when only one bit was set. Then 0x55555555 (binary 0101…0101) keeps only the even positions; if the bit survives the mask, it was at an even position.
steps: If n & (n − 1) is not 0, more than one bit is set: return false.
pitfalls: Only checking the power-of-two condition, which accepts 2, 8, 32.
Forgetting n > 0. In 32-bit arithmetic, −2³¹ & (−2³¹ − 1) is 0, so the minimum int looks like a power of two.
Using Math.log(n) / Math.log(4) and checking for an integer. Floating-point rounding makes that unreliable.

solutions.title: Divide by four
solutions.idea: Keep dividing by 4 while the number is divisible by 4. A power of four ends at exactly 1.

solutions.title: One bit, at an even position
solutions.idea: Powers of four have a single set bit, and it sits at an even position, which the mask 0x55555555 picks out.

followups: Another check: a power of two is a power of four exactly when (n − 1) % 3 === 0. Why?
Generalise: test for a power of 8 using bits.
